messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: double exponential
parts:
Hi!

Stan has the Laplace distribution built-in. I am about to throw this on a very large model and I was wondering how problematic this density is, given that the distribution has a discontinuous derivative at the mean. Does Stan do some tricks to smooth this out or is there another technique which gives me essentially the same, but with some trick to avoid the to-be-expected trouble due to the discontinuity.

Thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: double exponential
parts:
Hi Sebastian, 

here you find the Tricks Stan does: 
https://github.com/stan-dev/math/blob/develop/stan/math/prim/scal/prob/double_exponential_lpdf.hpp
fabs is used, which is correct.
Upps, find this already:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/HMtsTEpOg-w

Well if  you have a large model and using Laplace will get you also more run-time.
You could try to implement this cosh(x*alpha)*x and hope the autodiff will be faster.
I hope to specify my gradients by myself, since the time criticals I know or can figure
out. The rest could be handled by Stan autodiff.
Stan is the best MCMC around, so no complains, but I have to dig myself into this C++
type system again, which is a pain compared to other languages, like OCAML or Haskell
or live with it. 

Andre

Why did you need to dig into the type system? The function's documented.
The discontinuity problem is only worse than other sharp curves in that it
gets sharper the closer you get to zero, whereas something smooth will eventually
level off.

I love functional languages, but the upsides of C++ outweigh the benefit:

* matrix library Eigen
* math library Boost
* native(-ish) back-end for Python and R
* much larger developer base among statisticians and scientists

We're going through and adding doc and cleaning up a lot of the metaprogramming.
We were learning as we went the first time through, so it's a bit rough in
places.

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: double exponential
parts:
On Tuesday, February 21, 2017 at 11:12:23 AM UTC-5, Sebastian Weber wrote:
Thanks! I was looking for that as I remembered this was mentioned somewhere, but I did not find the right "google words".

Would it make sense to use what rstanarm has done also for the double exponential distribution definition in stan::math?

I don't think so. The function in the Stan Math library does what it is supposed to do, but when used in conjunction with NUTS, it can lead to poor MCMC estimates when the leapfrogger leaps over the discontinuity at zero. In a Stan program, you can introduce the scale-mixture parameter in the parameters block, define the thing that is supposed have a Laplace prior in transformed parameters, and then ignore the margins of the output that you do not care about.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: double exponential

Right --- we can't do sampling inside our function definition!

We could, though, define variables with built-in priors:

normal_real<mu, sigma> y;

and have that be equivalent to putting this in the parameters block

normal y;

and

y ~ normal(mu, sigma);

in the model block. Then all of a sudden our models would look
a lot more like other probabilistic programs. Like Michael, I'm
not convinced this kind of thing is a good idea.

- Bob
